responsive-layout-grid.text: A demo on the big screen, the founder hands their phone to an investor, and the pricing page has a third column hanging off the right edge with a horizontal scrollbar nobody can find. The layout was 'responsive' — on the developer's 27-inch monitor.

responsive-layout-grid.prompt: You want three cards side-by-side on desktop and stacked on mobile. Your instinct is a media query at 768px that flips display from flex-column to flex-row. What breaks between 320px and 768px — and at 769px on a narrow tablet? Answer before reading.
responsive-layout-grid.reveal: Everything in between is a guess. A single 768px breakpoint says nothing about 400px, 600px, or a 769px tablet held in portrait — the layout is correct at exactly two widths and unverified at every other. The grid way: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr))` lets the BROWSER compute how many 220px-minimum columns fit the actual width. One line, zero magic numbers, correct at every viewport — because the grid responds to space, not to a pixel you hardcoded.

responsive-layout-grid.text: The senior tell, and the WCAG 2.2 receipt: Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow, Level AA) requires content to be presentable without loss of information or functionality and without two-dimensional scrolling for vertically-scrolling content at a width of 320 CSS px, except where a two-dimensional layout is essential (e.g. maps, data tables). An intrinsic grid passes 1.4.10 by construction; a fixed-px grid fails it the moment the column is wider than the viewport. Reflow behavior is not just an aesthetic — WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow, Level AA) makes it an accessibility conformance requirement, and your state matrix is the evidence that you met it.

responsive-layout-grid.question: A reviewer says: 'Prove this layout is responsive, not just that it looks right on your screen.' Which response is the actual proof?
options: "It has a media query at 768px, so it's responsive."
"Here is the state matrix: at 320px it renders 1 column with no horizontal scroll, at 768px 2 columns, at 1440px 4 — all verified by resizing, and min-width:0 prevents the long-string overflow."
"It uses Flexbox, which is a modern layout system."
"It looks fine on my monitor and on the iPhone in dev tools."
responsive-layout-grid.explanation: Responsiveness is proven by behavior across viewports, not by the presence of a feature. Option 2 names the rendered result at each breakpoint, the WCAG 1.4.10 no-overflow check at 320px, and the specific line (min-width:0) that defends against the realistic failure — that is the evidence a reviewer can re-run. 'It has a media query' (1) and 'it uses Flexbox' (3) name tools, not outcomes; 'looks fine on my screen' (4) is exactly the happy-path claim the reviewer is challenging.

types-and-ui-contracts.outcome: Take one real component that fetches data (a profile card, an orders table, a search box) and write its UI contract: a discriminated-union state type that makes every reachable state — loading, empty, error, disabled, success — explicit and impossible to confuse, then a state matrix that proves each one renders an accessible, distinct surface.
types-and-ui-contracts.proof: component_state_matrix_and_accessibility_packet.md: a TypeScript state union where the compiler rejects illegal combinations (data present while loading, error and success at once), a 5-row state matrix (loading/empty/error/disabled/success → what renders + the a11y signal), and a note tying each error/empty state to a WCAG 2.2 success criterion. A reviewer reads the type and can name every state the UI can be in.
types-and-ui-contracts.unlock: Your state type is a discriminated union the compiler enforces, and your matrix maps all five states to a distinct, accessible rendering — no boolean soup.
types-and-ui-contracts.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a UI contract if your state is three loose booleans (isLoading, hasError, isEmpty). That permits illegal states like loading-and-error at once. A contract makes the illegal state unrepresentable — the type, not your discipline, forbids it.

types-and-ui-contracts.text: A blank white screen ships to production: the fetch failed, but the component only knew isLoading and data, so error fell through the cracks and rendered nothing. No spinner, no message, no retry — just a void a screen reader announces as an empty page. One missing state in the type, one user stranded.

A component's type is a promise about what it can be — and an unhandled state is a broken promise that surfaces as a blank screen, a frozen spinner, or a button users tab into but cannot use. Typing UI state as one explicit contract is the move that turns 'I think I handled the error case' into 'the compiler will not let me forget it.'

types-and-ui-contracts.prompt: A component holds `isLoading: boolean`, `data: User | null`, and `error: string | null`. How many distinct states can those three fields combine into — and how many are ones your UI should actually be in? Answer before reading on.
types-and-ui-contracts.reveal: Two booleans-plus-nullable give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 raw combinations, but only 4 are legal (loading, success, empty, error) — the other 4 are nonsense the type still permits: loading-with-data, error-with-data, loading-and-error together, all-null-forever. Every illegal combination is a bug waiting for production. A discriminated union collapses those 8 into exactly the states you allow, so the impossible ones cannot even be typed.

component-composition.text: The design review stalls on one screen: a single ProductCard component with 22 props, where `isLoading && !isError && hasData && !isDisabled` decides what renders, and nobody can answer 'what shows when the API is slow AND the user has no items?' The staff engineer deletes it and assembles five small pieces in its place — and suddenly every state has an obvious home.

Composition is how you keep a growing UI honest: instead of one component absorbing every variation through props and conditionals, you assemble small parts that each render one thing. It is the foundation the rest of this module builds on — form validation, error boundaries, and responsive layout all assume your UI is composed, not monolithic.

component-composition.reveal: Four booleans is the trap — they create 2^4 = 16 combinations, most of which are nonsense (loading AND disabled AND destructive?). The composition move: a single Button that accepts a `variant` and *children*, and lets the caller compose the spinner IN (`<Button><Spinner/> Saving…</Button>`). The button owns press behavior and focus ring; the caller owns content. Props configure; children compose. Reaching for another boolean is the smell that you should have opened a slot instead.

That red border is the entire difference between a sale and a support ticket.

Forms are where users hand you their money, their data, and their trust — and where the most accessibility lawsuits land. This lesson turns 'the field is wrong' into a perceivable, recoverable, keyboard-reachable state, the contract every real product form must meet.

forms-validation.prompt: Your email field is invalid, so you set its border to red and show red text below it. Is that field now accessibly validated? Decide before reading on.
forms-validation.reveal: No — on two counts. A screen reader announcing 'email, edit text' never mentions the error, because the red text is just nearby pixels, not programmatically tied to the input. And a colorblind or low-vision user may not perceive 'red' at all. Accessible validation needs aria-invalid='true' to mark the field broken, aria-describedby pointing at the error's id so the input OWNS the message, and a non-color signal (text + icon). The red border is the last 10% — the wiring is the skill.

Validating is the decision point: it runs every rule and branches. If a field breaks a rule, we drop into the Invalid state.
Invalid is where accessibility lives: aria-invalid flags the input, aria-describedby links its message, and role='alert' speaks the change.
The repair path matters as much as the failure. The user fixes the field, and we re-enter Validating to re-check.
When all rules pass, Validating hands off to Submitting, and the request goes to the server.
The server can reject: Server error carries the same aria wiring so failures stay perceivable, then retry loops back into Validating.
Or the server accepts and we reach Success. The invariant throughout: every error is bound to its field, or it is not validation.

api-client-contracts.prompt: `const data = await res.json()` — TypeScript happily lets you write `data.user.name`. So what is wrong with trusting that line? Answer before reading on.
api-client-contracts.reveal: `res.json()` is typed `any` (or `Promise<any>`) — TypeScript stops checking the moment the network boundary is crossed. `data.user.name` compiles even when the server sent `{ error: 'rate limited' }`. The type was a comforting fiction; at runtime the field is `undefined` and the render throws. A contract replaces the fiction with a parse: validate the bytes, THEN you have a real type.

storyboard.say: It starts here: the component needs data, so it calls the typed API client instead of fetching raw JSON itself.
The client reaches out over the network, fetching the response from the backend API.
The backend hands back raw JSON — untrusted, unshaped, exactly the thing that can silently rename a field.
At the edge, the response schema parses that JSON. This is the guardrail: shape is checked before anything reaches render.
When it matches, valid typed data flows back into the component and drives the success state.
When it doesn't match, the schema throws right there, routing into a designed, accessible error state that renders real error UI.
And if anything still slips through during render, the error boundary catches the uncaught throw — a blank white screen never ships.
The invariant: typed data in, typed failure out — parse at the edge and every downstream screen inherits designed failure instead of hope.

api-client-contracts.text: Standards grounding (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.1 and 4.1.3): the error state is not done when it renders red — it is done when it is identified in text and programmatically announced. A table with filters and pagination is the most common product surface there is — and the one where state, async, accessibility, and the URL all collide at once. Get the state model right here and you have the pattern for every list view, search page, and admin grid you will ever build.

tables-filters-pagination.prompt: Where should the active filter and current page number actually live — React component state (useState), or somewhere else? Decide before reading on.
tables-filters-pagination.reveal: Not component state — the URL. Filter and page are shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-able view state, so the query string (?status=refunded&page=4) is their real home. Put them in useState and you silently break refresh, deep links, the back button, and open-in-new-tab — four things users do constantly. The rule: if a teammate would want to paste the link in Slack and have it show the same view, it belongs in the URL, not the component.

steps: Predict the semantic and visible result before executing.

Identity comes from the URL: id is a route param passed in from app/orders/[id]/page.tsx — not a useState set by a row click. This single choice is what makes the surface deep-linkable and refresh-proof.
Fetch keyed by id: The query key includes id, so navigating to a different order refetches and caches per-order. queryFn resolves Order | null so 'not found' is data, not an exception.

Three weeks later they wonder why they never see that creator's posts. The button felt fast and was wrong, which is worse than slow and honest.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase of frontend engineering: the network is real, slow, and fails. Optimistic UI buys perceived speed by updating before the server confirms — but that speed is only safe if you can take it back, and only humane if every transition (pending, error, rollback) is visible to a screen reader and to the eye.

storyboard.say: It starts at the trigger button. A keyboard user presses Enter or Space to open the dialog, no mouse required.
When the dialog opens, focus must move IN and be contained inside it by a focus trap.
With the trap in place, Escape dismisses the dialog and restores focus back to the trigger the user came from.
Now the failure path. Skip the trap and Tab leaks past the dialog onto the page behind it.
And if Escape never restores focus, it falls to the bare body element, stranding the keyboard user on a screen they cannot leave.
The repair is the contained loop: focus in, trapped, Escape out, restored. Every control reachable, operable, and never a trap.
The lesson: prefer native elements. They grant logical Tab order, expected keys, and clean dismissal by default.

accessibility-keyboard.intro: Prove the component is keyboard-operable — mouse unplugged:
items: Tab to the control from the page top. If you cannot reach it without a mouse, it is not in the tab order — start from a native element.

Inside a composite widget (menu, tabs, listbox), Arrow keys move between items without leaving the widget.
Press Escape on any open overlay: it must close AND return focus to the trigger, not drop focus on <body>.
Confirm a visible focus indicator on every focusable element (WCAG 2.4.7) — Tab through and watch the ring move.
Run the Playwright keyboard flow: it drives Tab/Arrow/Enter/Escape only and asserts focus position. Green = proven.

storyboard.say: The PR says 'responsive — see screenshot.' But a component is never one thing: it's a grid of states crossed with viewports.
States run down as rows, viewports run across as columns. Every cell in that matrix is a separate claim about how the component behaves.
The happy path is easy to prove: success at 1440 is the cell that gets screenshotted and pasted into the PR.
But the failure hides in error at 320: the toast overflows the viewport and focus vanishes into a hidden node. Four failures, one desktop screenshot missed them.
The repair is to walk all cells: Playwright drives the real browser through every state and every breakpoint.
Each cell captured becomes evidence in the proof packet — a matrix of browser-captured screenshots a reviewer can re-run.
And the failing cell doesn't just get flagged — it's re-proven and folded back into the packet. The invariant: no cell unproven, no claim without a screenshot.

frontend-testing-strategy.text: The demo is flawless: type a query, results appear, ship it. In production the API is slow, then 500s, then returns zero rows — and the component renders a blank white box with a spinner that never stops, because nobody tested the four states that are not success.

This lesson sits in the synthesis phase of Frontend And Fullstack Product Engineering: you can already build component state, form validation, and accessible UI — now you prove they hold. The Frontend Testing Strategy turns 'it works on my machine' into a reviewable matrix that pins every UI state to a test at the cheapest layer that can fail honestly.

frontend-testing-strategy.prompt: Your component has five states: loading, empty, error, disabled, success. You write one test that types input and asserts results appear. How many of the five states did you just cover? Answer before reading on.
frontend-testing-strategy.reveal: One — success. The single happy-path test renders success and silently skips loading (does the spinner show and clear?), empty (zero-results message vs blank box?), error (does the error boundary catch the 500, or does React unmount the tree?), and disabled (is the submit button truly non-interactive, or just gray and still clickable?). Four of five states — the four users actually complain about — are untested. 'It works' meant 'one of five paths works.'

steps: Predict the semantic and visible result before executing.
Loading state: Assert the spinner exists AND carries role=status, so screen readers announce it. A spinner with no role is a happy-path spinner — sighted-only.
Empty state: Success with zero rows is its OWN state. Without this test, an empty array renders a blank box and the user assumes the app is broken.
Error state: Prove the error boundary catches the 500, renders an alert, and keeps the tree mounted with a retry. A 500 that unmounts React is the white screen of death.
Disabled state: Disabled must be REAL: assert toBeDisabled, then click it and assert nothing fired. A button that only looks gray but still submits is the classic disabled-in-name-only bug.

storyboard.say: The trophy is widest where testing is cheapest. Static types and lint catch typos and shape errors before a single test runs.
Climb up: unit tests pin pure logic, component tests prove rendered states, and E2E walks the real user journey.
The state matrix is the brain here. It lists every UI state and routes each to the cheapest layer that can fail honestly.
Four of five states land on the component layer: loading, disabled, success, and the ones you actually render.
Here is where production breaks: error and empty states get skipped, so the app renders a blank box with a spinner that never stops.
Visual regression and accessibility wrap every state, verifying keyboard and viewport behavior across the whole component.
The invariant: every UI state owns a test that can turn red. Untested is not passing, it is unknown until it breaks in prod.

frontend-testing-strategy.title: Testing the five states, one assertion at a time
frontend-testing-strategy.subtitle: The component-level suite that turns the state matrix into red-or-green — error and empty get tested, not just success.

steps.label: Loading state
steps.note: Assert the spinner exists AND carries role=status, so screen readers announce it. A spinner with no role is a happy-path spinner — sighted-only.

steps.label: Empty state
steps.note: Success with zero rows is its OWN state. Without this test, an empty array renders a blank box and the user assumes the app is broken.

steps.label: Error state
steps.note: Prove the error boundary catches the 500, renders an alert, and keeps the tree mounted with a retry. A 500 that unmounts React is the white screen of death.

steps.label: Disabled state
steps.note: Disabled must be REAL: assert toBeDisabled, then click it and assert nothing fired. A button that only looks gray but still submits is the classic disabled-in-name-only bug.

frontend-testing-strategy.caption: Four tests, four non-success states — each can return red on its own. The success path is the one you do not have to fight for; these are.

frontend-testing-strategy.text: WCAG 2.2 lives in the layer the happy path never reaches. The senior tell: their component suite tabs through the form by keyboard (focus order, visible focus ring, Enter submits), renders at a 320px viewport to catch overflow, and asserts role/aria on every state — because the user on a screen reader at 320px is exactly the user a happy-path test pretends does not exist. Grounded in WCAG 2.2 (w3.org/TR/WCAG22) and SWEBOK V4 verification.

frontend-testing-strategy.question: A reviewer says 'show me the exact evidence this isn't just a happy-path suite.' Which answer proves a real Frontend Testing Strategy?
options: 'CI is green and code coverage is 92%.'

'Here is the empty-state test asserting a no-results message, the error test asserting the boundary catches a 500 and keeps retry enabled, the disabled test that clicks and asserts nothing fired, plus a Playwright keyboard flow at 320px.'
'I tested the main user flow end to end in Playwright.'
'Every component renders without throwing when I open the app.'
frontend-testing-strategy.explanation: Only option 2 points to tests that can FAIL on the non-success states — empty, error, disabled — plus the keyboard + viewport check WCAG demands. Coverage % (1) can be 92% and still skip every error branch; one e2e flow (3) is still one path; render-without-throwing (4) is the weakest possible assertion. The proof is a red-capable test per state, not a green badge.

frontend-testing-strategy.intro: Prove your strategy tests more than success — no green-badge vibes:
items: Point to the test that fails if the empty state renders a blank box instead of a 'no results' message. If there is none, your success test is masking the empty state.
Point to the test that fails if a 500 unmounts the tree instead of hitting the error boundary. Force the mock to reject and watch it go red.
Click your disabled control inside a test and assert nothing fired — 'looks gray' is not 'is disabled'.
Run one Playwright flow with keyboard only: tab to the field, type, Enter to submit, and assert focus lands somewhere sane. WCAG 2.2 keyboard-operable is non-negotiable.
Render the component at a 320px viewport and assert no horizontal overflow. Note the screenshot. The narrowest real phone is the cheapest a11y regression to catch.

fullstack-integration-workflow.doNotClaim: Do not claim the workflow is integrated because the happy path renders. A workflow that only handles the 200 response is a demo, not an integration. If you cannot point to what the UI does on a 500, a slow response, and an empty result, the matrix has holes and the packet is not done.

fullstack-integration-workflow.text: The demo nailed it on stage: type, submit, green checkmark. In production the API times out, the spinner spins forever, the submit button is still live so the user double-posts, and a screen-reader user never hears that anything happened. The happy path was never the workflow — the other four states were.

Fullstack integration is the synthesis move of this course: it fuses component state, form validation, API behavior, and accessibility into one workflow the user can actually complete. The matrix is where those threads meet — Section 1 of the packet you carry into the capstone.

fullstack-integration-workflow.prompt: A form posts to /api/subscribe. You wire onSubmit to call the API and show a success toast on resolve. What is wrong before you have written a single bug?
fullstack-integration-workflow.reveal: You modeled one of five states. A POST can be in-flight (loading — and the button must disable to stop double-submits), rejected (error — the user needs the message and focus moved to it), or return nothing useful (empty). 'Resolve and toast' silently assumes the network is fast, never fails, and always returns data. The integration is the state matrix, not the call.

steps: Predict the semantic and visible result before executing.
The state machine, in the type: A discriminated union makes the five states exhaustive: the compiler will not let you forget 'empty' or 'error'. This is the matrix expressed as code.
Enter loading on every submit: Set loading BEFORE the await. This is what disables the button — the gap between click and response is exactly where double-submits happen.
A non-2xx is not success: fetch only rejects on network failure, so res.ok must be checked explicitly. Forgetting this is the single most common integration bug: a 500 sails into the success branch.
200 is not always content: A 200 with no created record is the EMPTY state, not success. Distinguishing empty from success is what separates an integration from a happy-path demo.
Catch maps failure to a user message: The error boundary of the workflow: timeouts, 5xx, and thrown errors all land here as a message the user can read — never a silent swallow.

State drives the announcement: aria-live='assertive' interrupts for errors; 'polite' for success. aria-busy + disabled stop the double-submit. The accessibility evidence is wired to the same status, so it can never drift from the UI.
Change one state or boundary and identify the exact regression evidence.

fullstack-integration-workflow.subtitle: One form-to-API workflow. The POST fans out into five states; the error and empty paths (often skipped) are first-class. aria-live carries each transition to assistive tech.

legend.label: in-flight — the state that disables submit
success — the only path most demos handle

storyboard.say: The workflow begins in idle: the form is valid, the button armed, waiting for a keyboard-reachable submit.
A valid submit fires POST /api/subscribe. This single request is the fork where five distinct outcomes are born.
The request goes in-flight. We enter Loading and immediately disable the button so a double-post is impossible.
The demo path: a 201 lands, Loading resolves to Success, the green checkmark the stage saw.
But the API can answer 200 with no result. Empty is a real state, not a blank Success screen.
And on 5xx or timeout we reach Error, then return to idle: re-enable the button, focus the message so it can't spin forever.
Every resolution flows to the aria-live region: Success announces politely, Error assertively, so a screen-reader user always hears the outcome.
The invariant: no state is unhandled. The happy path was never the workflow, the other four states are.

fullstack-integration-workflow.text: Standards grounding, not vibes: WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.3 (Status Messages) requires that a status change — 'subscribed', 'that email is already in use' — reach assistive tech WITHOUT moving focus, which is exactly what aria-live gives you. options: A screenshot of the green success toast after a valid submit.

The success screenshot (1) and the fetch-was-called test (4) only cover the path that was never in doubt; the backlog note (3) concedes the holes exist.
